answers.answer: Caching could replace the repeated 80 ms guide build with a 2 ms lookup for popular station-language pairs. Weekly changes suggest reuse is valuable, provided the team defines acceptable staleness. Use station-guide:{stationId}:{language}, because language changes the answer. On a hit the API returns the usable stored guide without that database lookup. On a miss the API reads/builds the guide from the authoritative database, writes the copy to the cache, and returns it; the cache does not fetch independently. A miss still pays the cache lookup, 80 ms database work, and cache write; storage and keeping copies current add costs. A hit can be stale.

evidence.quote: Creating the copy still costs work: fetch or compute the result, then write it to the cache. Storage, lookups and keeping copies current all have costs.
The application finds a usable entry under the requested key and returns the stored result.
No usable entry exists. The application reads the database, stores a copy in the cache and returns the result.
The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the result from the database on its own.
Include the inputs that change the answer.

answers.answer: C receives the old hours. Deletion happens before A stores its already-fetched old value, so A recreates a stale entry that C hits. Thus the team cannot claim every read after B finishes sees new hours. For this freshness-critical endpoint, bypass the cached hours and read the authoritative database for each request; under the stated commit prerequisite, a subsequent database read sees the committed update. This avoids serving this stale copy without designing a cache concurrency protocol.

evidence.quote: A reader can fetch $20 before the update, pause, then refill $20 after removal. The next cache hit still returns $20.
Invalidation alone does not guarantee freshness.
Keep freshness-critical decisions tied to authoritative data.

answers.answer: Case A: at 12:03 the original entry is still within its lifetime, so the request can use it even though the 12:02 source change makes it stale. At 12:11 it has expired at 12:10, so the request must fetch the source and refill. Case B: removal at 12:04 leaves no entry for 12:05, so that request must fetch the source despite the original ten-minute TTL not having elapsed. TTL bounds how long this entry may remain; it does not refresh at expiry, keep it current with source changes, promise ten minutes of residence, or bound the age of the source data used to fill it. Removal for memory is eviction, rather than expiration by elapsed lifetime.

evidence.quote: Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the data every minute; a later miss must load it again.
Removes entries to make room.
An entry can be evicted before its TTL ends.
TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of the source data used to fill it.

answers.answer: Use one shared cache entry: with no concurrent fills, deleting that entry removes the map every instance would look up, and a later miss reloads from the database. Today each lookup occurs inside its API process; deleting one local copy leaves the other three untouched, so requests to those instances can receive their old map. A shared lookup goes over the network to a separate service, costing the accepted 2 ms and requiring service operation. Losing one local cache affects only its instance; other instances keep their copies. If the shared service is unreachable, all four lose access to its entries. Sharing simplifies this deletion goal but does not itself keep the database and cache synchronized.

evidence.quote: Lives inside each API process. Reads avoid a network call, but each process fills and updates its own copy. Their copies can reflect different versions of the same data.
Several API servers use a separate cache service, such as Redis or Memcached. They can reuse entries, but each lookup adds a network call and the service needs operating.
Restarting one API process discards its local cache; other processes keep their copies. If the shared cache is unreachable, every API server using it loses access to those cached entries.
Sharing reduces separate copies. It does not automatically keep the cache current with the database.

answers.answer: After expiration, concurrent misses can each repeat the same schedule read and exceed the database's 500 reads/second capacity. Coalesce readers for that key: one starts the database lookup and concurrent readers share its in-progress result, which is then cached, reducing many identical reads to one lookup for that group. A whole-cache outage can redirect nearly 10,000 requests/second to a database that handles only 500. Cap total fallback schedule reads across instances at no more than its safe capacity and reject excess requests with the permitted temporary error; this bounds database work instead of allowing each request to trigger a read. If an accessible last-known schedule is available, return it only within the permitted 60 seconds, avoiding database work for those requests; otherwise use the bounded fallback/error path. The lesson does not specify where to retain an outage-accessible stale copy, so its availability cannot be assumed. Test the empty and unavailable cache cases.

evidence.quote: Many requests miss the same key together and repeat its database lookup. Coalescing requests lets concurrent readers share one in-progress lookup.

A cache outage can turn most reads into database traffic. Limit fallback work to what the database can handle; reject excess requests or serve older data only where the application permits stale results.
Test with an empty or unavailable cache. A warm cache can hide insufficient database capacity.

answers.answer: Do not add this cache now. Each result is read exactly once, so filling it after that read cannot save a later read: there is no reuse. The 2 ms database read already fits the 100 ms budget, and ten reads/second is comfortably within the given capacity. Filling adds cache writes and storage, and a cache-aside lookup would add another operation without producing useful hits; managing another copy also adds cost. Reconsider if repeated reads of the same result become common enough to avoid substantial database work, with acceptable staleness; measure response time, database load, hits, and miss costs to confirm the benefit.

evidence.quote: Choose results that are expensive enough to obtain, frequently reused and able to tolerate a defined amount of staleness.
If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.
Creating the copy still costs work: fetch or compute the result, then write it to the cache. Storage, lookups and keeping copies current all have costs.
Compare response time and database load before and after caching. Track hit ratio, the fraction of lookups served from the cache, and the cost of misses.
